<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#A1.SS3" title="In Appendix A Prompt Templates ‣ WorkflowPerturb: Calibrated Stress Tests for Evaluating Multi-Agent Workflow Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">A.3 </span>Description Change Prompt</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#A1.SS4" title="In Appendix A Prompt Templates ‣ WorkflowPerturb: Calibrated Stress Tests for Evaluating Multi-Agent Workflow Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">A.4 </span>Iterative Refinement Prompt (Error Injection)</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#A1.SS5" title="In Appendix A Prompt Templates ‣ WorkflowPerturb: Calibrated Stress Tests for Evaluating Multi-Agent Workflow Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">A.5 </span>Iterative Refinement and Escalation</span></a></li>
</ol></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_appendix"><a href="#A2" title="In WorkflowPerturb: Calibrated Stress Tests for Evaluating Multi-Agent Workflow Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">B </span>Detailed Metric Definitions</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_appendix">

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WorkflowPerturb</span>: Calibrated Stress Tests for Evaluating Multi-Agent Workflow Metrics</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Madhav Kanda
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
</span></span></span></span>

</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">

</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">

</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Microsoft
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">

</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Microsoft
</span></span></span></span>

<span class="ltx_personname">Sharad Agarwal
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Microsoft
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">LLM-based systems increasingly generate structured workflows for complex tasks. In practice, automatic evaluation of these workflows is difficult, because metric scores are often not calibrated, and score changes do not directly communicate the severity of workflow degradation.
We introduce <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WorkflowPerturb</span>, a controlled benchmark for studying workflow evaluation metrics. It works by applying realistic, controlled perturbations to golden workflows.
<span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WorkflowPerturb</span> contains 4,973 golden workflows and 44,757 perturbed variants across three perturbation types (Missing Steps, Compressed Steps, and Description Changes), each applied at severity levels of 10%, 30%, and 50%.
We benchmark multiple metric families and analyze their sensitivity and calibration using expected score trajectories and residuals.
Our results characterize systematic differences across metric families and support severity-aware interpretation of workflow evaluation scores. Our dataset will be released upon acceptance.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para ltx_align_bottom">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center" style="width:345.0pt;"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"></span></p>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate multi-step, dependency-rich workflows for high-stakes settings, where failures can have real operational or scientific consequences. Such workflows now appear in scientific automation, biomedical information access, enterprise copilots, and cloud and DevOps assistants <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bran et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jin et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Microsoft (2026)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chandrashekar (2025)</a></cite>. In these settings, correctness depends not only on wording but on ordered dependencies and the presence of critical steps.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Evaluating these workflows remains unexpectedly difficult. Existing workflow metrics each capture only a narrow slice of correctness: lexical metrics fail under paraphrasing, structural metrics may overlook semantic drift, and semantic metrics can assign favorable scores to workflows missing critical steps. A central practical challenge is calibration: it is often unclear what a score means in terms of functional risk. For example, does a drop from 0.90 to 0.84 reflect harmless rephrasing or the loss of an essential dependency? Without calibrated interpretation, metric values are difficult to use for regression testing, model comparison, or automated filtering.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">With the widespread deployment of LLM-generated workflows in industry, incorrect or degraded workflows can have severe consequences. In cloud and DevOps settings, flawed orchestration may lead to outages or misconfigured infrastructure; in scientific and biomedical domains, subtle workflow deviations can alter analytical conclusions. Production systems are also dynamic: models are deprecated and upgraded, for example under Azure OpenAI model retirement policies<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
          <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-foundry/openai/concepts/model-retirements" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-foundry/openai/concepts/model-retirements</a></span></span></span>, orchestration libraries evolve, and engineers revise prompts and agent definitions. Each such change may alter workflow structure or semantics. This raises a core practical question: how can we determine whether a modified workflow remains functionally equivalent to a validated reference? How can such checks be integrated into CI/CD pipelines without manual review? At the heart of this problem lies reliable workflow evaluation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To make this concrete, consider a validated production workflow for deploying a service, including resource provisioning, access controls, deployment, and observability configuration. An LLM-generated workflow may preserve terminology while omitting access hardening, compressing observability into a vague step, or reordering dependencies. Many metrics still assign high scores due to surface overlap or coarse structural similarity, leaving engineers uncertain whether deviations are benign or dangerous.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To address these challenges, we introduce <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WorkflowPerturb</span>, a benchmark of over 44,000 workflows constructed through controlled perturbations. We generate three perturbation types, Missing Steps, Compressed Steps, and Description Changes, each applied at graded intensity levels of 10%, 30%, and 50%. These structured degradations enable systematic analysis of metric calibration under known severity, revealing which metrics are robust to benign edits, which fail under functional degradation, and how workflow scores can be interpreted more reliably in production settings.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Agentic evaluation and tool-use benchmarks.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent work has focused on evaluating large language models in agentic and tool-using settings, where models must select, invoke, and sequence external functions. The Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Patil et al. (2025)</a></cite> provides a standardized benchmark for evaluating LLMs on realistic function-calling tasks, emphasizing correctness of tool selection, and execution outcomes, and moving beyond single-turn generation to end-to-end task success in tool-augmented environments. While BFCL evaluates agent performance through execution success, it does not study how automatic evaluation metrics behave under different types or severities of workflow degradation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Diagnosing agent failures from execution traces.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Several recent approaches analyze execution trajectories to diagnose and localize agent failures. AGENTRX <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Barke et al. (2026)</a></cite> examines agent execution traces consisting of intermediate actions, tool calls, and environment feedback to identify failure causes and error propagation. TRAIL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deshpande et al. (2025)</a></cite> similarly uses trace-based reasoning over structured action sequences and intermediate states to localize issues in agent execution. These methods operate on runtime execution traces and assume access to environment interactions and task outcomes. Our setting differs in that we do not rely on execution traces or success signals; instead, we study static workflow representations and evaluate how automatic metrics respond when workflows deviate from golden references in controlled and graded ways, enabling systematic analysis of metric calibration, sensitivity, and blind spots.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span><span id="S3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WorkflowPerturb</span></h2>

<figure id="S3.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17990v1/plots/main-fig.png" id="S3.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/268;" width="476" height="268" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Real-world example illustrating perturbations in LLM-generated workflows for a customer support escalation task.
<span id="S3.F1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Missing Steps:</span> The <span id="S3.F1.10" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;">red node</span>, present in the original workflow, is omitted in the LLM-generated version.
<span id="S3.F1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Compressed Steps:</span> The <span id="S3.F1.12" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;">red</span> and <span id="S3.F1.13" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;">blue nodes</span> from the original workflow are merged into a single <span id="S3.F1.14" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;">blue node</span>, reducing workflow granularity.
<span id="S3.F1.15" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Description Change:</span> All nodes retain the same semantic meaning as the original but differ in syntactic phrasing.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We model a workflow as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G=(V,E)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>V</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G=(V,E)</annotation></semantics></math>, where each node <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v\in V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v\in V</annotation></semantics></math> represents a step described in natural language and each edge <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(u,v)\in E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi>E</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(u,v)\in E</annotation></semantics></math> denotes a precedence constraint. Given a golden workflow <math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>G</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G</annotation></semantics></math> and a candidate workflow <math id="S3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>G</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math>, an evaluation metric produces a score <math id="S3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s(G,G^{\prime})\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>G</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s(G,G^{\prime})\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> (or a normalized variant) intended to reflect workflow quality or similarity. Rather than proposing a new workflow generator, our focus is to analyze <em id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">metric behavior</em>: under controlled degradations of known severity, do metric scores change in an interpretable and calibrated manner? We study this question by introducing structured perturbation types, graded severity levels, and an expected score trajectory that characterizes how an ideal metric should respond as workflow quality degrades</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Benchmark Construction</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Source Data.</span>
We begin with the set of workflows in WORFBENCH <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qiao et al. (2024)</a></cite> and retain those with <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lvert V\rvert\geq 5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lvert V\rvert\geq 5</annotation></semantics></math> nodes. This threshold ensures each workflow has enough steps to meaningfully perturb and evaluate metric sensitivity.
<br class="ltx_break"></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Perturbation Patterns.</span>
Through exploratory analysis of LLM-generated workflows, we identified several issues that degrade workflow quality, among which three recurring patterns emerged. We model these patterns as controlled perturbations applied to golden-standard workflows:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Missing Steps:</span> LLM-generated workflows often omit essential actions that are required for complete task execution.
Such omissions result in incomplete or truncated execution paths when compared to the golden workflow.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Compressed Steps:</span> Generated workflows frequently contain fewer nodes than their golden counterparts, condensing multiple fine-grained actions into a single broader step.
While this may preserve most of the content, it alters the structural properties of the workflow and leads to mismatches under graph-based evaluation.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Description Changes:</span> Even when workflows preserve the correct structure, step descriptions often differ syntactically from the golden reference.
This creates lexical variation that can confuse surface-level metrics while retaining semantic meaning.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17990v1/plots/percent-perturb-new.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/204;" width="381" height="204" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Visualization of <span id="S3.F2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Missing Steps</span> perturbations applied to the six-node blog generation workflow.
At each level, a proportional number of nodes is randomly dropped: 1 node (10%), 2 nodes (30%), and 3 nodes (50%).
Higher perturbation levels result in increasingly incomplete workflows that diverge from the golden sequence.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Functional Implications of Perturbations.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Although <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WorkflowPerturb</span> evaluates static workflow representations, the perturbations are designed to reflect realistic failure modes with potential execution-level consequences. Missing steps may eliminate required actions, leading to incomplete or failed task execution. Compressed steps can merge distinct tool invocations or dependency boundaries, potentially altering execution order or granularity. In contrast, description changes preserve structural dependencies but may introduce semantic ambiguity. Our objective is to study how automatic metrics respond to these controlled degradations; evaluating their downstream execution impact is complementary future work.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To systematically study the impact of these issues on evaluation metrics, we apply each perturbation type at three severity levels <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{10\%,30\%,50\%\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{10\%,30\%,50\%\}</annotation></semantics></math> of the nodes in the golden workflow are affected as illustrated in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Benchmark Construction ‣ 3 WorkflowPerturb ‣ WorkflowPerturb: Calibrated Stress Tests for Evaluating Multi-Agent Workflow Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. These graded levels not only mimic realistic variations observed in practice but also allow us to probe the calibration of metrics, i.e., whether metric scores degrade proportionally with increasing perturbation severity.
<br class="ltx_break"></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Perturbation Generation and Validation.</span>
For each workflow and perturbation configuration, we employ large language models to generate variants. To ensure correctness, each variant undergoes automated static validation checks:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S3.I2" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S3.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Node Count Consistency:</span> Given a golden workflow with 10 nodes, applying a 10% removal perturbation must produce a workflow with precisely 9 nodes. Any deviation from this expected count is flagged as inconsistent. The nodes selected for removal are chosen randomly.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Change Count Verification:</span> For a <math id="S3.I2.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30\%</annotation></semantics></math> perturbation, exactly <math id="S3.I2.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math> nodes must be altered, either removed, compressed, expanded, or paraphrased. If fewer or more nodes are modified, the output is rejected. For removal and compression operations, the results are verified by comparing the number of nodes before and after the perturbation. For paraphrasing, we explicitly pass the specific nodes to be paraphrased to ensure that exactly the required number of nodes are modified.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">These checks target the two most common generation failure modes: (i) deleting or merging too many nodes, and (ii) over- or under-applying paraphrasing. All prompt templates used in this stage along with our iterative refinement strategy are documented in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Prompt Templates ‣ WorkflowPerturb: Calibrated Stress Tests for Evaluating Multi-Agent Workflow Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>. 
<br class="ltx_break"></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Structured Paraphrasing for Description Changes.</span>
For the description-change perturbation, we do not rely on unconstrained paraphrasing, which often introduces hallucinations. Instead, we explicitly pre-select <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha\times|V_{\text{golden}}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mtext>golden</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha\times|V_{\text{golden}}|</annotation></semantics></math> nodes (where <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0.1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5\}</annotation></semantics></math>) for paraphrasing. The model is instructed to only rephrase the text of those nodes without adding or removing factual content. For example, a step such as <em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">“Check server logs for errors”</em> may be paraphrased to <em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p6.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">“Inspect the server log files for error entries”</em>, while the graph structure and node set remain unchanged. 
<br class="ltx_break"></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dataset Statistics.</span>
The final <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WorkflowPerturb</span> corpus contains approximately 4,973 golden workflows, and <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="44{,}757" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>44,757</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">44{,}757</annotation></semantics></math> perturbed variants spanning three perturbation patterns and three severity levels. All variants pass automated validation, and a subset was manually inspected to verify perturbation correctness.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Score Assignment and Perturbation Alignment.</span>
Each workflow is assigned a score reflecting perturbation severity, with lower scores indicating deviation from the golden workflow. For <em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p8.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Missing Steps</em> and <em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p8.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Compressed Steps</em>, the score equals the remaining workflow fraction, computed as <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-p</annotation></semantics></math> for perturbation percentage <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> (e.g., <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p{=}30\%\rightarrow 0.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0.7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p{=}30\%\rightarrow 0.7</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p{=}50\%\rightarrow 0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p{=}50\%\rightarrow 0.5</annotation></semantics></math>). In the case of Compressed Steps, this decrease is justified by the loss of structural granularity: multiple fine-grained actions (often corresponding to distinct tool invocations) are merged into broader nodes, violating the one-tool-per-step abstraction and reducing fidelity to the golden execution graph. For <em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p8.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Description Changes</em>, the score remains constant across severity levels, since these edits affect only textual descriptions and not the underlying workflow structure.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Metrics</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate seven metrics spanning structural, lexical, semantic, order-based, and judgment-based families. Structural metrics (Graph F1, Chain F1) measure topological consistency via subgraph matching and sequence alignment. Lexical metrics (BLEU, GLEU) compute n-gram overlap. BERTScore measures contextual embedding similarity. Kendall’s <math id="S4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> evaluates rank-order consistency. LLM-as-Judge provides rubric-based holistic assessment. Full definitions are provided in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Detailed Metric Definitions ‣ WorkflowPerturb: Calibrated Stress Tests for Evaluating Multi-Agent Workflow Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Structural Metrics</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Chain F1.</span>
Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qiao et al. (2024)</a></cite>, predicted node chains are aligned with valid topological orderings of the golden workflow, and the longest increasing subsequence (LIS) is computed. Precision and recall are defined as
<math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{chain}}=l/|V_{\text{pred}}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>chain</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mtext>pred</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{chain}}=l/|V_{\text{pred}}|</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{\text{chain}}=l/|V_{\text{golden}}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mtext>chain</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mtext>golden</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{\text{chain}}=l/|V_{\text{golden}}|</annotation></semantics></math>,
where <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> is the LIS length. The final score is their harmonic mean (F1).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Graph F1.</span>
The predicted and golden workflow graphs are aligned using a Maximum Common Induced Subgraph (MCIS) algorithm. If the largest shared subgraph contains <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> nodes, precision and recall are defined as
<math id="S4.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{graph}}=k/|V_{\text{pred}}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>graph</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mtext>pred</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{graph}}=k/|V_{\text{pred}}|</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="S4.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{\text{graph}}=k/|V_{\text{golden}}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mtext>graph</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mtext>golden</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{\text{graph}}=k/|V_{\text{golden}}|</annotation></semantics></math>. The score is their harmonic mean (F1).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Lexical Metrics</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">BLEU</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Papineni et al. (2002)</a></cite>
is a precision-oriented <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>-gram matching metric with a brevity penalty, while
<span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GLEU</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Napoles et al. (2015)</a></cite>
balances <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>-gram precision and recall and is more robust for shorter or paraphrased step descriptions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Semantic Metric</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">BERTScore</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2020)</a></cite>
compares contextual embeddings of step descriptions from pretrained transformer models and computes precision, recall, and F1 via token-level cosine similarity.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Ordering Metric</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Kendall’s <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math></span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kendall (1938)</a></cite>
measures rank correlation between generated and gold step orderings, defined as
<math id="S4.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=(C-D)/\bigl(\tfrac{1}{2}n(n-1)\bigr)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=(C-D)/\bigl(\tfrac{1}{2}n(n-1)\bigr)</annotation></semantics></math>,
where <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> are the numbers of concordant and discordant pairs among <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> aligned steps. Scores range from <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>LLM-as-Judge</h3>

<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To complement automatic metrics, we use an <em id="S4.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">LLM-as-Judge</em> evaluation with GPT-4o (Azure OpenAI). The model is prompted with the task description, golden workflow, generated workflow, and a rubric defining 0–5 scores covering correctness, completeness, ordering, and clarity, with anchor examples.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Results and Analysis</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate metric behavior across perturbation types and severities, assigning each workflow a predefined degradation score for interpretability. All reported <em id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">LLM-as-Judge</em> scores are linearly normalized from the original 0–5 scale to the [0,1] range for comparability across metrics.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Overall trends.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Across all perturbation types, metric scores generally decrease as perturbation severity increases, confirming that the benchmark introduces progressively harder deviations from the golden workflows. However, degradation patterns differ substantially across metric families. Structural metrics (Graph F1, Chain F1) track structural distortions closely, lexical metrics (BLEU, GLEU) are highly sensitive to token-level variation, embedding-based similarity (BERTScore) is less sensitive to structural perturbations because it does not directly encode graph completeness, while ordering-based metrics (Kendall’s <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>) mainly change when perturbations alter relative step precedence (e.g., via compression or deletion). LLM-as-Judge captures broader notions of functional correctness and completeness.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17990v1/Missing-step.svg" id="S5.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/262;" width="476" height="262"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Metric scores across perturbation levels (mean <math id="S5.F3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> std) for Missing Steps.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Missing Steps.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Figure <a href="#S5.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ Overall trends. ‣ 5 Results and Analysis ‣ WorkflowPerturb: Calibrated Stress Tests for Evaluating Multi-Agent Workflow Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and Table <a href="#A3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Appendix C Results Discussion ‣ WorkflowPerturb: Calibrated Stress Tests for Evaluating Multi-Agent Workflow Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, removing steps disrupts workflow completeness and dependency structure. Structural metrics degrade nearly linearly with higher removal rates (Graph F1 and Chain F1: <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.90\rightarrow 0.61" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.90</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0.61</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.90\rightarrow 0.61</annotation></semantics></math>), closely tracking the imposed severity. Lexical metrics exhibit sharper drops (BLEU: <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.79\rightarrow 0.29" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.79</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0.29</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.79\rightarrow 0.29</annotation></semantics></math>; GLEU: <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.80\rightarrow 0.42" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.80</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0.42</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.80\rightarrow 0.42</annotation></semantics></math>), reflecting substantial token loss when steps are deleted. BERTScore decreases overall (0.81 → 0.72), though the trajectory is slightly non-monotonic between 30% and 50%, reflecting embedding-level tolerance to partial deletion. Kendall’s <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> declines from <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.81" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.81</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.81</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.44" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.44</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.44</annotation></semantics></math>, appropriately penalizing disrupted execution order. LLM-as-Judge drops <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.64</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.64</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.32</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.32</annotation></semantics></math>, indicating strong sensitivity to missing functional content.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17990v1/Compressed-step.svg" id="S5.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/262;" width="476" height="262"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Metric scores across perturbation levels (mean <math id="S5.F4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> std) for Compressed Steps.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Compressed Steps.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S5.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Missing Steps. ‣ 5 Results and Analysis ‣ WorkflowPerturb: Calibrated Stress Tests for Evaluating Multi-Agent Workflow Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, and Table <a href="#A3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Appendix C Results Discussion ‣ WorkflowPerturb: Calibrated Stress Tests for Evaluating Multi-Agent Workflow Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> illustrates the effect of merging fine-grained actions into broader steps. Structural scores again decrease substantially (Graph F1: <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.86\rightarrow 0.45" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.86</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0.45</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.86\rightarrow 0.45</annotation></semantics></math>; Chain F1: <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.86\rightarrow 0.44" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.86</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0.44</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.86\rightarrow 0.44</annotation></semantics></math>), reflecting altered connectivity and reduced graph fidelity. Lexical metrics decline from <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.87\rightarrow 0.51" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.87</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0.51</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.87\rightarrow 0.51</annotation></semantics></math> (BLEU) and <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.86\rightarrow 0.53" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.86</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0.53</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.86\rightarrow 0.53</annotation></semantics></math> (GLEU), as merged descriptions reduce direct n-gram overlap. Notably, BERTScore is already relatively low at mild compression and decreases slightly (<math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.41\rightarrow 0.32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.41</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0.32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.41\rightarrow 0.32</annotation></semantics></math>), suggesting that embedding similarity is sensitive to abstraction and merged semantics. Kendall’s <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> shows pronounced degradation (<math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.74\rightarrow 0.17" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.74</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0.17</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.74\rightarrow 0.17</annotation></semantics></math>), indicating substantial disruption of pairwise precedence relations under compression. LLM-as-Judge declines from <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.64</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.64</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.37" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.37</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.37</annotation></semantics></math>, reflecting loss of procedural granularity even when high-level intent is partially preserved.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17990v1/Description-Change.svg" id="S5.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/262;" width="476" height="262"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Metric scores across perturbation levels (mean <math id="S5.F5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> std) for Description Changes.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Description Changes.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">When only textual descriptions are modified (Figure <a href="#S5.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Compressed Steps. ‣ 5 Results and Analysis ‣ WorkflowPerturb: Calibrated Stress Tests for Evaluating Multi-Agent Workflow Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, and Table <a href="#A3.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Appendix C Results Discussion ‣ WorkflowPerturb: Calibrated Stress Tests for Evaluating Multi-Agent Workflow Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), the underlying graph structure remains intact. Structural metrics therefore remain stable (Graph F1: <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.97\rightarrow 0.85" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.97</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0.85</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.97\rightarrow 0.85</annotation></semantics></math>; Chain F1: <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.96\rightarrow 0.85" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.96</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0.85</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.96\rightarrow 0.85</annotation></semantics></math>), showing only minor sensitivity to indirect structure–text interactions. Lexical metrics decline with heavier paraphrasing (BLEU: <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.85\rightarrow 0.50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.85</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0.50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.85\rightarrow 0.50</annotation></semantics></math>; GLEU: <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.86\rightarrow 0.52" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.86</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0.52</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.86\rightarrow 0.52</annotation></semantics></math>), as expected under surface-level variation. In contrast to structural perturbations, BERTScore remains high (<math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.94\rightarrow 0.79" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.94</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0.79</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.94\rightarrow 0.79</annotation></semantics></math>), indicating that semantic similarity is largely preserved under controlled rewriting. Kendall’s <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> remains nearly unchanged (<math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.00\rightarrow 0.99" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.00</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0.99</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.00\rightarrow 0.99</annotation></semantics></math>), consistent with preserved ordering. LLM-as-Judge scores remain high and stable (<math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.98" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.98</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.98</annotation></semantics></math>), reflecting that functional correctness is largely unaffected by paraphrasing.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, no single metric captures all failure modes. Structural metrics reliably detect missing or compressed steps but remain insensitive to purely textual edits, whereas lexical metrics are highly responsive to paraphrasing yet can over-penalize structural deletions. Embedding-based and judgment-based metrics provide complementary signals with distinct calibration properties. A more detailed sensitivity analysis is provided in Appendix <a href="#A3.SS1" title="C.1 Sensitivity Analysis ‣ Appendix C Results Discussion ‣ WorkflowPerturb: Calibrated Stress Tests for Evaluating Multi-Agent Workflow Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Key Insights and Practical Guidance</h2>

<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Workflow validation under change.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In industrial settings, workflows frequently evolve due to model upgrades, prompt revisions, or orchestration library changes. Our results show that different metric families respond differently to structural versus textual changes. Structural metrics are reliable indicators of missing or compressed steps, making them suitable for detecting functional regressions when workflows are modified. Lexical metrics detect paraphrasing but may over-penalize deletions. LLM-as-Judge provides a holistic signal aligned with perceived workflow quality but introduces variance. These distinctions are critical when validating workflow updates.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">CI/CD integration.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">WorkflowPerturb enables severity-aware calibration of evaluation metrics, allowing practitioners to interpret scores relative to expected degradation patterns. In a CI/CD pipeline, candidate workflows generated after model or orchestration updates can be compared against approved golden workflows using a calibrated metric bundle. Deviations beyond empirically validated thresholds can automatically trigger review or rollback. By understanding which metrics are sensitive to which failure modes, automated validation pipelines can be configured to prioritize structural regressions while tolerating benign paraphrasing.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Metric selection in practice.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">No single metric suffices across all perturbation types. We recommend reporting a compact bundle of complementary metrics and interpreting them jointly with respect to perturbation severity. WorkflowPerturb provides a controlled testbed for selecting and calibrating such metric bundles before deployment.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduced <span id="S7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WorkflowPerturb</span>, a benchmark for evaluating workflow evaluation metrics under controlled structural and textual perturbations. Our analysis reveals that commonly used metrics exhibit distinct sensitivity patterns and calibration gaps across failure modes. These findings highlight the importance of severity-aware interpretation when validating workflow updates in production systems. By enabling calibration and metric selection, WorkflowPerturb provides practical support for automated workflow validation in CI/CD pipelines and evolving LLM-driven platforms.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Prompt Templates</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The following prompts were used to generate perturbed workflow variants. Placeholders in curly braces {} denote the specified perturbation type or severity level.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Missing Step Prompt</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<blockquote id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_quote">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Given the following workflow, please <span id="A1.SS1.p1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">remove exactly {10%, 30%, 50%}</span> of its steps.
Return only the modified workflow as a numbered list of steps, preserving the order of the remaining steps.
Do not add or paraphrase any content.</span></p>
</blockquote>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Compressed Step Prompt</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<blockquote id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_quote">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Given the following workflow, please <span id="A1.SS2.p1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">merge consecutive steps until exactly {10%, 30%, 50%}</span> of the original steps are merged.
Each merged step should concisely describe the actions of the combined steps.
Return only the modified workflow as a numbered list of steps.
Do not remove or paraphrase steps outside the merged groups.</span></p>
</blockquote>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Description Change Prompt</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<blockquote id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_quote">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS3.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Given the following workflow, please <span id="A1.SS3.p1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">paraphrase the descriptions of exactly {10%, 30%, 50%}</span> of its steps.
Ensure that the meaning of each paraphrased step remains unchanged.
Do not remove, merge, or add any steps.
Return only the modified workflow as a numbered list of steps.</span></p>
</blockquote>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.4 </span>Iterative Refinement Prompt (Error Injection)</h3>

<div id="A1.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">When a generated output fails validation, we re-inject the error message into the prompt. For example:</p>
<blockquote id="A1.SS4.p1.2" class="ltx_quote">
<p id="A1.SS4.p1.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS4.p1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Your output had 8 nodes instead of 9 for a 10% removal.
Please regenerate the workflow and ensure that exactly one node is removed.
Return only the modified workflow as a numbered list of steps.</span></p>
</blockquote>
<p id="A1.SS4.p1.3" class="ltx_p">This process is repeated up to three times per model before escalation to a stronger model.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.5 </span>Iterative Refinement and Escalation</h3>

<div id="A1.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Variants failing validation enter a feedback-driven refinement loop. The validation error is explicitly injected back into the next prompt. For example:</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<blockquote id="A1.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_quote">
<p id="A1.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS5.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">“Your output had 8 nodes instead of 9 for a 10% removal. Please regenerate the workflow and ensure exactly one node is removed.”</span></p>
</blockquote>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">If the corrected output again fails validation (e.g., paraphrased 4 nodes instead of 3), the process is repeated up to three times. After three unsuccessful iterations, the task is escalated to a more reliable generation method.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Detailed Metric Definitions</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present the formal definitions and implementation details of all evaluation metrics used in <span id="A2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WorkflowPerturb</span>. Where applicable, we include equations and illustrative examples showing how the scores are computed.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Chain F1</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Suppose the predicted node chain is <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C(V^{p})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>p</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C(V^{p})</annotation></semantics></math> and the gold workflow graph is <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G(V^{g},E^{g})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>g</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>E</mi><mi>g</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G(V^{g},E^{g})</annotation></semantics></math>.
From <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>G</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G</annotation></semantics></math>, we can enumerate all possible topological orderings <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{C(V^{g})_{1},C(V^{g})_{2},\ldots\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>g</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>g</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{C(V^{g})_{1},C(V^{g})_{2},\ldots\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The predicted chain is compared against each ordering using the <em id="A2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS)</em>:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<table id="A2.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l_{i}=\text{LIS}(C(V^{g})_{i},C(V^{p}))," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>l</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>LIS</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>g</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>p</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l_{i}=\text{LIS}(C(V^{g})_{i},C(V^{p})),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">and the longest valid subsequence length is taken as</p>
<table id="A2.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l=\max(|l_{1}|,|l_{2}|,\ldots,|l_{n}|)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>l</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l=\max(|l_{1}|,|l_{2}|,\ldots,|l_{n}|).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Precision and recall are then</p>
<table id="A2.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{chain}}=\frac{l}{|V^{p}|},\qquad r_{\text{chain}}=\frac{l}{|V^{g}|}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>chain</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>l</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>p</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mtext>chain</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>l</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>g</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{chain}}=\frac{l}{|V^{p}|},\qquad r_{\text{chain}}=\frac{l}{|V^{g}|},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">yielding</p>
<table id="A2.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{1}^{\text{chain}}=\frac{2\,p_{\text{chain}}\,r_{\text{chain}}}{p_{\text{chain}}+r_{\text{chain}}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn><mtext>chain</mtext></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>chain</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mtext>chain</mtext></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>chain</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mtext>chain</mtext></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{1}^{\text{chain}}=\frac{2\,p_{\text{chain}}\,r_{\text{chain}}}{p_{\text{chain}}+r_{\text{chain}}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
